headline: The K–12 Classroom Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet students and parents, give times, pages and grades, describe how a student is, ask and answer simple school questions, make polite requests, and ask for help when you don't understand, and start K–12 Classroom Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Say classroom words clearly and greet students and parents at school.
lessons.focus: The five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr and the written accent in classroom words; greetings

words.note: Say every vowel clearly: es-cu-e-la. Spanish vowels stay short and pure.
For a man: el maestro. Students also say "maestra" to call the teacher.
The accent marks the stressed syllable: sa-LÓN.
Stress LÁ. The z sounds like English s in Mexico.
ch sounds like the ch in "church."
The h is silent; j sounds like a strong English h: O-ha.
ll sounds like English y: SI-ya.
rr is a strong rolled r; the single r at the end is a light tap.
Common in Mexico for the whiteboard or chalkboard. Stress the last syllable: rrÓN.
Use from about noon until dark.
A male teacher says: Soy el maestro Torres.
To a man: Mucho gusto, señor.
Niños covers a mixed group of boys and girls.

lessons.speaking: Greet a parent at the classroom door, say your name and that you are the teacher, and point to the backpack, chair and board.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Give class times, page numbers, minutes and test scores to students and parents.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time with a las, and school quantities: pages, minutes, points, grades

words.note: ¿A qué hora? means "at what time?"
El grado is the year in school (tercer grado). A score is la calificación.

words.es: Abran el libro en la página 45.
words.note: Abran is the command to the whole class (ustedes).

words.en: Your daughter got 92 on the test.
words.es: Su hija sacó 92 en el examen.
words.note: Sacar is the everyday verb for getting a score.
Use es la for 1:00: Es la 1:00.

lessons.speaking: Tell a parent what time class starts, when recess and lunch are, and what score their child got on the test.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Describe who a student is and how they feel today, and say where someone is at school.
lessons.focus: ser for who or what someone is, estar for feelings, conditions and location

words.note: estar listo = ready; ser listo = clever. Use lista for a girl.
For a woman: la directora.

words.es: Soy la maestra de tercer grado.
words.note: ser: who you are. A man says: Soy el maestro.

words.en: Your daughter is in the nurse's office.
words.es: Su hija está en la enfermería.
words.note: estar: where someone is.
For a girl: Es una alumna nueva.
Informal tú, to a boy. To a girl: ¿Estás lista?

words.en: The principal is in the office.
words.es: La directora está en la oficina.

words.en: Your son is a very good student.
words.es: Su hijo es muy buen estudiante.

lessons.speaking: Tell a parent that you are their child's teacher, that the child is a good student, and how the child is today: tired, sick or happy.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Say what students have and need, ask what they want, and say what has to be done.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive with school supplies

words.note: Mexico: los colores. Crayons are las crayolas.
Informal tú, to one student.

words.en: You have to bring the notebook tomorrow.
words.es: Hay que traer el cuaderno mañana.
words.note: hay que + infinitive: something everyone has to do.
In Mexico a school meeting is una junta.

words.en: Your son needs a red folder.
words.es: Su hijo necesita una carpeta roja.

lessons.speaking: Ask a student if they have their homework and notebook, and tell a parent what supplies the class needs this week.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Tell students where the class is going, what you will do next, and what they can do.
lessons.focus: ir, ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer and poder around the school building

words.note: Many Mexican families also say el camión.
Say en casa for at home and a casa for going home.

words.en: Can I go to the restroom?
words.note: Students ask this all day. al = a + el.

words.en: Tomorrow we're going to take a test.
words.es: Mañana vamos a hacer un examen.
words.note: ir a + infinitive: a plan.
Hagan is the command to the whole class (ustedes).

words.en: The bus is going to arrive at 3:10.
words.es: El autobús va a llegar a las 3:10.

lessons.speaking: Tell your class to line up, say where you are all going next, and answer a student who asks to go to the restroom.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Describe what you and your students do in class each day and each week.
lessons.focus: Present tense of regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs for yo, tú, usted, nosotros and ellos

words.note: In Mexico el grupo also means a class section, like 3.° A.
Los lunes means every Monday.

words.en: We read a story every day.
words.es: Leemos un cuento todos los días.
words.note: -er verb, nosotros: leemos.
-ir verb, tú: escribes.
-ar verb, ellos: trabajan.

words.en: I speak English and a little Spanish.
words.es: Hablo inglés y un poco de español.

words.en: You get an email every Friday.
words.es: Usted recibe un correo cada viernes.
words.note: Formal usted, to a parent.

lessons.speaking: Explain your class schedule to a parent: what the students read, write and study each day, and when they eat lunch.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask students and parents simple questions about names, places, times and reasons.
lessons.focus: Question words qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué and cuál with rising questions

words.note: For more than one person: ¿quiénes?
Use cuántas with feminine nouns: ¿cuántas páginas?
Two words in a question; the answer porque (because) is one word.
Use cuál before es to ask which one: ¿Cuál es tu salón?
Informal tú, to a student.

words.en: When can you come to the school?
words.note: Formal usted, to a parent.

lessons.speaking: Ask a new student their name, where their backpack is, and how many pages they read, then ask a parent when they can come in.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say what a student has not done yet, what never happens, and ask for more or less.
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, más, menos and otro with absences and homework

words.note: Spanish uses a double negative: No tengo nada.
Never say un otro. Use otra with feminine nouns: otra hoja.
Common in Mexican schools for a late arrival.

words.en: Your son hasn't turned in the homework yet.
words.es: Su hijo todavía no entrega la tarea.

words.en: Nobody leaves the room without permission.
words.es: Nadie sale del salón sin permiso.

words.en: You need to read more at home.
Do you want another sheet of paper?

lessons.speaking: Tell a parent their child has not turned in the homework yet, has no tardies, and needs to read more at home.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Politely ask a parent to sign, call, check or send something for school.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede…? + infinitive and usted commands (llame, revise, mande, escriba) with parents

words.note: Los padres means mother and father. Schools also say los padres de familia.
Full form in Mexico: la boleta de calificaciones.
Also la hoja de permiso.
Short for el correo electrónico.

words.en: Can you sign the report card, please?
words.note: Formal usted: polite with every parent.

words.en: Can you come to a meeting on Tuesday?
words.es: ¿Puede venir a una junta el martes?
Llame a la escuela mañana, por favor.
words.note: Usted command of llamar.

words.en: Send a note if your daughter is absent.
words.es: Mande un recado si su hija falta.
words.note: Mandar is the everyday Mexican verb for send.

words.es: Escriba su número de teléfono aquí.

lessons.speaking: Ask a parent to sign the report card and the permission slip, write their phone number, and come to a meeting next week.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize school cognates and ask for help or an interpreter when you don't understand.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad and -ente, and survival phrases for getting help

words.note: -ción words are feminine and match English -tion.
-dad words are feminine and match English -ty.
For a girl: la estudiante. The word stays the same.
Students answer "¡Presente!" when you take attendance.
For a woman: la intérprete.

words.en: I don't understand, can you repeat that?
How do you say "grade" in Spanish?

lessons.speaking: Tell a parent you are learning Spanish, ask them to speak more slowly or repeat, and offer an interpreter for the meeting.
